chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Today's topic is numerical computation for deep learning.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Basic idea of numerical computation is that we need to be very careful about the way that we handle real numbers in a few different contexts.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: One is if we use an algorithm that has to do some kind of careful representation of real numbers with a finite number of bits.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Real numbers like pi have infinitely many digits and then when we represent them in a computer we usually use 32-bit floating point numbers as an approximation for real numbers when we implement a deep learning algorithm on GPU.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: The use of 32 bits to represent something that really has infinitely many digits can often cause errors and we'd like to try to minimize the amount of damage to our program that happens when we use that representation.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Another consideration for numerical computation is how sensitive a function is to very small changes in its input.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: This comes up even if we were able to theoretically use real numbers without having to represent them in 32 bits.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: When we do things like optimize a function, if that function is very sensitive to little tiny changes in the input, it becomes a lot harder to search for the inputs that minimize that function because little tiny changes in our search can strongly influence the outcome of the search.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: As a brief roadmap for today, I'm going to cover two different topics. The first is iterative optimization, how we actually make algorithms that search for the minimal point of some function and how this gets affected by numerical considerations.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Next I'm going to talk about rounding error underflow and overflow. How the use of 32 bits to represent real numbers can affect deep learning programs.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Starting out with iterative optimization, we're going to cover three different topics here. The first is how the gradient descent algorithm works. The second is curvature, the idea that the functions are optimizing are non-linear and how the second order curvature of these functions affects the optimization process.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Finally, we'll have a few comments on constrained optimization. The basic algorithm that we use for most iterative optimization is gradient descent.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: I've illustrated this here with a really simple function, f of x equals 1.5x squared. You can see it plotted with the dashed blue light that I'm highlighting with my mouse cursor.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If we would like to minimize this function, we can do it by following the gradient. Let's say that x is greater than 0. The gradient in this case, because the function is one dimensional, is just the derivative.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So the derivative can be represented by the value f prime of x. Over here, f prime of x, represented by the green line, is positive. So if we descend the gradient by moving in the opposite direction of the derivative.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Everywhere that we're over here, where the green line is positive, gradient descent will move left and downhill. So starting here, we would trace the blue curve leftward until we reach its minimum point here.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Where the derivative is 0, we are no longer told by the derivative to move in any particular direction. So we stop.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If we started over here on the left side, over here, the derivative is negative. And we move in opposite the direction of the derivative. So we would actually apply positive updates to our input x.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And we would move rightward along the function x squared until we reach the minimum and stop where the derivative is equal to 0.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: I've described a gradient descent basically in terms of this idea that we move downhill until we find a point where the derivative is 0.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And the example of f of x equals 1 half x squared, there was only one point like that. In reality, there might be a lot of different points that have zero derivatives.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Here I've drawn a function that's very squiggly and has several different local minima. Local minima are points that are smaller than in f of x value than all the other points surrounding them, but they're not necessarily the lowest point overall.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So here, if we look to the left or the right of this point, we go uphill a little bit. If you go further to the left, we can find much lower points.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Usually in the context of deep learning, we can't really expect to find this global minimum over here. We might want to do that, but it's probably not feasible.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: In practice, we often give up and find a point more like this one here. It's a local minimum, but the value of f of x is actually very low.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So we've done a good job of reducing the value of the function, even if we don't find our way all the way to the bottom of the function.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: In practice, we don't even necessarily find a local minimum. In practice, we often just sort of get stuck for numerical reasons, and that's the topic of this chapter.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: I'm fast forwarding a little bit, and I'm showing you a figure from chapter 8. On the x-axis, I show you how long gradient descent has been running on a particular problem.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: In the two different plots, I show you two different things. On the left side, I show you how big the gradients are over time, specifically I'm plotting the norm of the gradient.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Every little black dot is a different step of the gradient descent algorithm. So you can see it's kind of noisy. On different steps, it's not like we always see the same gradient norm twice in a row. It bounces around a lot.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: But I've fit a smooth blue curve to these lines. You can see how the gradient norm actually gradually gets bigger over time.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Based on the plots that I showed you on the previous slides, you might expect that the gradient norm would shrink as you approach a local minimum and it can graduate go down to zero.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: It turns out that a lot of the time we actually just get stuck and can't really keep making progress toward regions of smaller gradient norm.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So we stop when f of x has become very small rather than when the gradient has gone away.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: You could say maybe this plot that I made here where I show the gradient getting bigger over time, maybe that's an example of failure, maybe the algorithm is just broken.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: But actually if we look at the plot on the right, I'm showing you the error rate of a classifier that we're training with gradient descent.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And this error rate decreases over time successfully and levels off to about state of the art accuracy for the problem that this is training on.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So you can see that this is actually an example of the optimization algorithm succeeding from our point of view. It's not actually finding a local minimum.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: It's just finding a very low value of the function f of x that are minimizing and that low value turns out to be good enough for us to use the model.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Someone has asked why don't we test a larger diversity when we've reached the local minimum wouldn't that tell us we could get a lower elsewhere.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And the answer is yes, a lot of the time we do things like run multiple random restarts of the optimization algorithm.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And sometimes you can find lower values that way. For a lot of problems, you also find that several different random restarts end up with about the same the same final value.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Someone else asked, can you please explain gradient norm a bit? The basic idea is if you have an input to your function x with multiple coordinates, then the gradient gives you the derivative of your function with respect to each of those coordinates.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And that tells us the direction we should go in to move downhill. If you measure the norm of that gradient, that gives you an idea of how steep the function is. It tells you how quickly you can expect the function to drop if you move in a specific direction.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: I'm going to skip the next question because it's answered later in the talk. And then there's one more question about how can the gradient increase when you are using a descent direction? Is it not convex?

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: It turns out that the gradient can increase if you optimize a neural net because the function is not convex. It's also possible that if you use too large of a step size, the gradient can increase because you move to a region that's steeper.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: I think of the way that we optimize deep learning functions as more of a way of life than a strictly mathematical discipline right now.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If you approach optimization from a really pure math point of view, you're usually looking to do something like find literally the smallest value of some function f of x.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Or you might have some other formally defined criterion like you're looking for a critical point of f of x where the value is locally the smallest in some neighborhood.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: For deep learning, we usually have a more qualitative pragmatic approach where our goal is to just decrease the value of f of x a lot.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And we aren't necessarily hoping to actually find even a local minimum. We just want to make the error rate go down until the error rate is low enough that our model can be used for some engineering application.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Actually finding a critical point might be very difficult and a lot of the critical points we find may not be what we want.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: The next topic in our overview of iterative optimization is the effective curvature on these optimization algorithms.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We've mentioned that gradient descent in theory will approach a critical point where the gradient is equal to zero.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Here I show you three different kinds of critical points in one dimension.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: There can be a minimum where the function curves upward around the critical point and the critical point is thus lower in value than a critical point.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: There can also be a local maximum where the function curves downward so the critical point is higher in value than all the surrounding points.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Or you can have saddle points where you actually are neither a minimum nor a maximum.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Settle points make a little bit more sense in two dimensions. You can think of it as there's one axis where the critical point is a local minimum and another axis where the critical point is a local maximum.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Local maximum are usually not much of a problem for optimization algorithms.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: The saddle points can be a problem for iterative optimization algorithms.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: There's one algorithm called the Newton's method where the basic strategy is to solve for a point where the gradient is equal to zero.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If you're able to solve that problem algebraically you can jump to a solution right away.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Unfortunately a solution in terms of Newton's method is not always actually a minimum.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If you have a function that has saddle points in it these are also places where the gradient is zero.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: But they are not really a minimum because they're a maximum across some axes.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So algorithms like Newton's method will accidentally teleport onto saddle points and get stuck.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: It turns out that for neural networks there are a lot more saddle points than local minimum.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Fortunately saddle points are not a big problem for gradient descent.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Unless you initialize directly on the saddle point gradient descent can escape the saddle point.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If you look at appendix C of a paper called qualitatively characterizing neural network optimization problems I have some math there where I show why gradient descent is able to escape.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We can characterize all of these different critical points by using curvature.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: As I said a local minimum is where the function curves up around around the point and the local maximum is where it curves down.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We can also think of this as a way of predicting how well gradient descent will perform.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Gradient descent basically says we're going to look at the slope of the function and we're going to pretend that the function is linear nearby our current x value.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And then we're going to move in a direction that will make our linear approximation go downhill.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: The amount of actual payoff that you get from that depends on how curved the function is.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If your function is perfectly linear, if you make a linear approximation to the function then it will just overlay the function exactly.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So here you can see I've got this dashed green line overlaying the blue line.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If we take a little step according to the direction of the derivative we're going to decrease the function f of x by exactly the same amount that our linear function predicted.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And that means that these iterative search algorithms where we always just take little steps moving downhill are going to work really well regardless of the size of step that we use.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If we have negative curvature where the function curves downward as you move away from the current point then we're actually in a very nice situation where if we take a little step of the curve, we're going to take a little step of the curve.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If we take a step that was predicted to reduce the dashed green linear function approximating f of x will find that f of x actually decreases even more than our approximation predicted to do to do.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So if we can find directions of negative curvature there a good way to reduce the value of the function very quickly.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Unfortunately what happens a lot more often is we have directions of positive curvature with directions of positive curvature the function curves up relative to the linear function.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So we have two small steps we end up not nearly decreasing the function as much as we wanted to.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And in fact if we take two big of a step we can accidentally increase the function value we can overshoot the minimum in this direction and go back uphill.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: That's why we start looking at what's called the numerics of the function we look at how much curvature there is to this function and see how it affects our ability to take large steps to search for the minimum value of the function.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Someone asked what was the name of the paper that I just told you can actually see that in the slides they're available at deep learning book.org.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So far I've shown you these one dimensional examples of curvature but in practice x is an end dimensional vector and we need to understand how the curvature affects the function in many different directions.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We can do that using the Hessian matrix the Hessian matrix is a matrix containing all of the second derivatives.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So if you look at row i and column j of the Hessian matrix you'll find the derivative where first we take the derivative and direct with respect to x i and next we take the derivative with respect to x j.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: It turns out that you can use the Hessian matrix to compute the second derivative in a particular direction d.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: You can do that by computing d transpose hd where d is a unit vector describing the direction where you would like to get the second derivative.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: It turns out that there's actually some nice intuition for what second derivative you'll get.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Hessian matrices are usually symmetric assuming that different properties of the function are held and a symmetric real valued matrix has an eigen decomposition in terms of orthogonal eigenvectors and eigenvalues associated with each eigenvector.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So you can write all of the eigenvectors in a matrix q and they become this orthogonal basis for the space that you're in and then you have a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If we look back at some of the slides from chapter two we can see what happens when we multiply by a matrix that has particular eigenvectors and eigenvalues.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If we start out with a bunch of points that are represented by this blue circle here and we multiply each of these points by a matrix that has eigenvectors v1 and v2.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We'll see that each of the points get stretched away from the origin according to the eigenvalues of the matrix.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So if you have a large lambda one eigenvalue associated with v1 you'll actually stretch out the circle in this direction.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Points will get pulled further out by a factor of lambda one.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And then if you have a small eigenvalue associated with direction v2 points will get pulled inward.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So you can see that these directions will be when you multiply h by d, d will either get stretched or shrunk according to how big or small the eigenvalues of the Hessian are in that direction.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And then when you take the dot product with the direction again you'll end up just measuring the size of that vector.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So you'll end up saying that the second derivative is based on how much the Hessian shrinks or stretches your vector in that particular direction.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: But what happens if your direction is not an eigenvector?

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Well then it turns out that you basically interpolate based on the eigenvectors that are nearby.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: You can compute the second derivative as a sum over all the different eigenvalues.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And you multiply by this term that measures how similar the direction you're looking in is to that corresponding eigenvalue.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: You can kind of see that in this plot that if you have a direction that's very closely aligned with eigenvector two, you're going to get your directions stretched by approximately eigenvalue two.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And then as you move towards eigenvalue one, the amount that your direction gets stretched is going to scale gradually up to the amount of stretching that comes from eigenvalue one.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If you're never going to stretch more than the maximum eigenvalue, you're never going to stretch less than the minimum eigenvalue.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We can use these eigenvalues to figure out what the optimal step size is likely to be.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So first off, if we have a direction of negative curvature, even a second order approximation would tell us that we can keep stepping forever.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: That's probably not going to be true for a neural net because it's very non-linear, very, it's not even really quadratic.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: It's likely to start going back uphill at some point for a large step size.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: The main place where the Hessian tells us a lot of information is if we look at the case of positive curvature, we know that if we start following the linear function downhill, we can decrease the value of the function.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: But if we step too far, we'll start to go back uphill. We don't want to step any further than this minimum point here.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We can make a second order Taylor series approximation to the value that we'll get when we take a specific gradient step.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We can say we're starting off at some point x0 and we're taking a gradient descent step where we move by step size epsilon multiplied by a gradient g.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: The first order Taylor series approximation, or second order Taylor series approximation tells us that the value at this new point will be approximately equal to the value at our current point.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Minus epsilon times the squared norm of the gradient. This is the first order Taylor series term.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Plus one half epsilon squared times the gradient multiplied by the Hessian multiplied by the gradient.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: This here is the directional second derivative in the direction of the gradient, but also scaled by the size of the gradient.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So if we then solve this equation for the minimum predicted value that we'll get after the step, we solve it in terms of the step size.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Assuming that we're looking in a direction of positive curvature, we find that the optimal step size is equal to the squared norm of the gradient divided by g transpose hg.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So what does this tell us overall? The numerator says that if the gradient is bigger, we can take bigger steps.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So big gradients will speed up the optimization algorithm.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: In the denominator, we actually see that this g transpose hg term can shrink the optimal step size a lot.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So if the gradient happens to point in a direction that's aligned with an eigenvector of the Hessian that has a big eigenvalue, you have to slow down a lot.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Otherwise, we'll overshoot the minimum and go back up hill.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Overall, this shows us something about why when we actually run an iterative search in practice, we may not actually arrive at a critical point.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Over time, we'd expect the gradient to get smaller and smaller, but we'll often also find for the kinds of optimization problems that come up with neural nets.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We'll find that this g transpose hg term gets very big and we're just not able to make very big steps anymore, even if the gradient remains large.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We can measure this with something called the condition number. The condition number looks at the largest ratio we can find between two of our eigenvalues.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If there's a very large eigenvalue and a very small eigenvalue, it means that when our gradient points in the direction of the large eigenvalue, we're forced to take very small steps.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We have to do that even if sometimes the gradient would point in the direction of a small eigenvalue and it would be safe to take larger steps.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Basically, if there's a wide range of eigenvalues, gradient descent has to miss out on a lot of the potential value that it could find on each step.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: It has to keep the step size small to avoid accidentally going up hill.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: You can see this with this contour plot. Here we're minimizing a quadratic function. Each of the black rings shows a set of points where the function is set.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: The function is of equal value. At the middle here, we've got a minimum of the function. Every time we see a ring on our way out, we're taking a step up in value of the function.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: The red path is showing how gradient descent moves.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Ideally, gradient descent would want to just point straight at the minimum and go straight there.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Instead, we keep finding that the gradients tend to point across this canyon.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We keep going down the canyon wall, overshooting the bottom of the canyon and coming to the other side of the canyon.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We're going this zigzagging fashion where we're always walking up or down a canyon wall instead of flowing down along the bottom of the canyon.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: You can see this with neural networks. That same paper that I mentioned earlier includes this visualization of a little 3D representation of what happens in a neural net optimization problem with the gradient descent.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: We can see that towards the end of training, gradient descent, as represented by this blue path, is moving down this really tight canyon with the green 3D mesh.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: The gradient is actually still pretty large here, but the curvature is even larger and the curvature makes it really hard to take large steps.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Some things about this visualization are a little bit hard to understand because when you work with multiple dimensions and project them down to just a few dimensions, some things can be lost.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: So one thing that we can't see here is that this blue curve is actually zigzagging a lot, just like in the previous visualization.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: It's just that the way that we made this plot means that we can't actually see the other dimensions where it's zigzagging.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: But those zigzags are stopping it from moving a lot faster along the bottom of this canyon.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: The last topic that we'll cover for iterative optimization is the idea of constrained optimization.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: And I don't actually have a lot to say about this. I'm just going to very quickly mention a little bit about how it works.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: If you have constraints for a function, like if you have some values, g, that measure some, how much you deviate from exactly satisfying a constraint or some values, h, that measure how far you are on the wrong side of some inequality, you can actually take your original function, f of x, and transform it into this new function called the Lagrangian function.

chunks.title: deep_learning_high_res
chunks.text: Where you penalize the function for violating those constraints.
